items.rationale: A toothpick that comes out clean or with a few dry crumbs shows the inside has set; wet batter clinging to it means the center is still raw, and a bit of flour stuck to the pick is not a real test result either.

items.answer: it springs back when you press it lightly in the center
accepted: the top springs back when lightly pressed
it pulls away from the sides of the pan
the edges pull away from the pan
items.rationale: A done cake springs back from a light touch instead of leaving a dent, and it also starts pulling away from the pan's sides; either is a valid second sign besides the toothpick.

Too much leavener makes the gas bubbles grow too large, so they merge and burst even in a cake that tested done, and the middle collapses as it cools. Blaming too long in the oven mixes up the cause of a dry cake with the cause of a sunken one.
When the oven runs too hot, the outside of the cake sets into a shell while the center is still rising, so the center has nowhere to go but up, cracking the top into a dome.

items.answer: it was overbaked, left in the oven too long or baked too hot
accepted: it stayed in the oven too long
items.rationale: Extra time in the oven, or an oven running hotter than the recipe assumes, bakes the extra moisture out of the crumb even when every ingredient amount was right.
A toothpick only reports on the spot it goes into, and the edges of a cake bake faster than the middle, so a clean test near the edge can still miss a middle that is underbaked.
